This game.. oh, this game. 
I don't usually write these reviews, mostly because the comment sections are all filled with ridiculous statements or just funny things to be said. But with this game.. I just couldn't /not/ write out my honest opinion for this game. 
You play as a man named Isaac. You're not a soldier, you're not a hero. You're an engineer who wound up on a zombie infested ship while trying to look for his girlfriend. 
This game has everything I could ever want out of a scary game. Even now, after playing through it thousands of times on the playstation 3, even the dismemberment Demo.

[h1][b]Aged Like Fine Wine[/b][/h1]
Dead Space is now more than 13 years old, but don’t let its age and dated graphics fool you. Some may say that I’m too late to the party, but I dare say that this game was truly ahead of its time, and there isn't anything like this nowadays. If you, like me, are new to the franchise or just looking for a good horror title, this review is for you - with no spoilers.

[h2]Curiosity in Storytelling[/h2]
You play as the silent engineer, Isaac Clarke, on his mission to repair the mining spacecraft USG Ishimura. Throughout the campaign, you will find leftover data like text and video logs explaining a fraction of events before your arrival. The variety of information given to you is like a piece of fabric, so you can sew the story back together just enough to understand what had and is happening. From data research regarding the “creatures” you encounter, to the sheer panic and the slow downward spiral into insanity that the crew had experienced due to the influence of “the artifact”. While the game's progress is linear, as you move from one section of the ship to another, everything still feels interconnected. There are some chapters where you return to the previous areas, the environment has been renewed, you can now enter previously-locked rooms, whereas some of the old segments are now blocked because of the advancement of the “creatures”.

[h2]Everything is Designed to Scare You[/h2]
The “creatures”, called Necromorphs, that you fight from the beginning to the end are heavily disfigured and mutated monstrosities you have never seen before! Each type of Necromorph you encounter is properly introduced and has build-up tension, whether through their faraway distinct screams, crawling in the vent to stalk you, or a few pieces belonging to a bigger, whole Necromorph, harassing you before its actual full appearance. Don’t let these grotesque creatures close their gap on you, as they will tear you asunder in the horrifying death scenes!
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2668026593
The Necromorph isn’t the only thing that terrifies you though. There are numerous instances where just the lightning and ambiance are enough to spook you to the point of being paranoid that something will attack you. Regardless if this is just the game design choice or a way of storytelling where “the artifact” causes you to hallucinate like the crew beforehand, it certainly does a great job messing with you.

For a game this old, the lightning and meshes of the environment aged very well. The textures are surely dated, but everything else synergizes so perfectly that walking alone in the ship without any enemies still sends a chill up my spine.

That being said, there are a few cheap jumpscares with no tension at all. There’s no build-up indicating that the creatures are coming to you, everything is quiet, then suddenly they appear out of nowhere, and the music just screeches loudly like in a typical horror movie.

[h2]Strategic Dismemberment - Simple but Unique[/h2]
In most shooters, you need to aim for the head for maximum damage or even a one-shot kill. If you do that in Dead Space, however, you’re gonna have a bad time or even hinder your progress due to ammo scarcity in higher difficulties. Necromorphs will attack in the most violent ways without any regard to their body like their former victims. The only way to kill them for good is to tear them apart by cutting off their limbs, appendages, or glowing weak points. Lore wise, they don’t need their head anymore, flesh and bones have been repurposed to become deadly blades. Gameplay-wise, it’s one of the most unique features in any shooter, now you have to re-learn how to aim for the limbs, and it’s also a nice break from the typical “headshot does the most damage” in video games.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BPWABzrD-_4
[h2]Guns? More like Overpowered Mining Tools![/h2]
Nearly all of the weapons you collect are tools used in mining for cutting and obliterating rocks, which are perfect for dismembering the limbs of your foes. If you have trouble aiming, use Stasis - an assistant tool used to work with fast-moving machinery - to slow them down for an easier aim. You can also briefly stun them by throwing objects with your Kinesis module - a tool used to pull objects towards you. There are a decent variety of weapons to keep multiple playthroughs enjoyable and nonrepetitive, like the Contact Beam, or a “shotgun” called Force Gun that forcibly blows almost everything away at point-blank range. They all have (dis)advantages in every situation: your trusty Plasma Cutter can put you through the entire game with ease, provided that you have another backup weapon for crowd-control.

As these tools can be upgraded to be perhaps too powerful, the game will be less challenging the further you progress. Even though the monsters are stronger and appear more often in packs, they still can’t stop Isaac because of his arsenals. The tension, the need for ammo management wear down fast as you progress with more abundant credits - Dead Space’s currency - to buy ammunition so much that you won’t have to worry about running out of it like in the first few chapters. Once you have fully upgraded the Pulse Rifle - the only military-grade weapon, this game is just a walk in the park.

[h2]No-pause menu? It’s called RIG[/h2]
This is probably the best feature that no other game can top off. Dead Space introduces a new kind of no-pause menu that was ahead of its time, and it’s called Resource Integration Gear, or RIG for short. It’s essentially an unstopping menu built into your upgradeable suit that’s compact and easy to navigate. The best thing is that it still lets you freely move your camera and walk around. Any incoming dialogue or video calls from other characters will be played in the background in real-time instead of quitting the menu.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2668036214
[h3]Performance, Encountered Bugs and Solutions[/h3]
[u]Specs: i5-10400F at 55°C, 16GB RAM DDR4, GTX 1650S 4GB at 68°C, Win 11[/u]
Dead Space runs smoothly as expected at the highest settings with consistent 60FPS. For an old game like this, I expected bugs, and here’s how I fix them:
[list]
    [*]Horrendous mouse control. That’s the first thing you notice when walking and aiming, it’s sluggish, inconsistent, and hard to use where precision is needed. Fixed with this:
https://community.pcgamingwiki.com/files/file/840-dead-space-mouse-fix/
    [*]Stuttering frame rates. Just simply disable in-game V-Sync, and enable V-Sync externally through the NVIDIA Control Panel.
    [*]Unplayable in Windowed Mode. While it uncaps the limited 60FPS in fullscreen, the actual gameplay is horrible. Isaac moves slowly with lagging like I’m having latency, with melee also suffering from the same issue. Pressing B to find an objective path spins the screen like crazy. I even got stuck and couldn't progress once, because a character disappeared when they’re supposed to be there, and the game didn’t spawn any enemies to fight. Just play in full screen instead.
    [*]Saved games’ difficulty changed when pressing “Continue Game”. My first playthrough's save slots have been lowered from Hard to Medium, and I didn’t realize it until it was too late. Always use “Load Game” to avoid this risk.
[/list]
[h1][b]Final rating: 8.5/10, a must-have for any horror lovers out there[/b][/h1]
If you are completely new to the horror genre and looking for one to get to know, Dead Space is the perfect entry for you. This title is worth its cheap full price thanks to the experience, but just wait for a sale, you will love it!

This game is old, it came out nearly 20 years ago. Yes it has some problems, that's an unfortunate reality with most games this old and definitely older. But, there are really simple fixes, and it doesn't take a rocket scientist to do! 

Download this patch to fix the horrible mouse issues ---> https://community.pcgamingwiki.com/files/file/840-dead-space-mouse-fix/ 
Just follow the instructions, you can't really screw this up!

Then, the game glitches HARD when playing at high frame rates. Bodies will be flying, doors might not open, it's a mess. DO NOT TURN ON IN GAME V-SYNC! 

Turning v-sync on through game will fix the weird physics issues, but it will also lock you at 30 fps. Instead, use your control panel to force v-sync on and lock it at 60 fps. Now the game works and you won't have a headache looking at it. You COULD try your luck with a higher frame rate, but don't try pushing it to 120 or higher. 60 is the safe spot.

And that's it! the game is now perfectly playable, and any issues you have with the game after this should be purely game play related! Because again, this game is nearly 20 years old. If you don't like a lot of the jank in controls with older games, what are you doing here? They released a remake of this game that's pretty good too, go buy that if you want a MODERN experience.

There are two problems with this game that easily can be fixed. First, we have the bug door in the beginning of the game. This bug seems to only occur when the game is running at an FPS higher than your monitor's maximum. To fix this, do not enable V-sync in-game (which is horrible), rather, open up the Nvidia control panel (sorry AMD users, I can't help you) and navigate to 3D settings -> Manage 3D settings -> Program settings. Once there, find the Dead Space.exe and set "Vertical sync" to on, "Triple buffering" to on and finally "Texture filtering - trilinear optimization" to on. This will only affect Dead Space, and fixes the door bug, without you having to enable V-sync in the game!

The other problem is that with awkward mouse controls, e.g. unchangable mouse acceleration. To enable raw input: go to this site: https://community.pcgamingwiki.com/files/file/840-dead-space-mouse-fix/. Download: "SteamDB entry", extract the file "dinput8.dll" from the downloaded file and put it in your main game (Dead Space) folder, e.g. C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Dead Space". Start the game, and you now have no mouse acceleration and can actually change the mouse sensitivity normally in-game.

Dead Space is an absolute master craft of Action Horror. It took all the right notes from RE4, expanded and improved upon the basics such as camera control and aiming, and of course with it's own unique setting and method of combat: it ended up being one of the most iconic games in it's genre. 

To this day it remains one of my favorite Action Horror games. It's execution of horror elements at times feels lacking (an over reliance on jump scares, for example), but the look and aggression of the necromorphs, the brutality of the combat as you hack limbs apart and try to get some breathing room- It just comes together to create a really tense combat loop. 

The game has some issues running on modern PCs, but they can be fixed pretty easily in my experience. I don't think the lackluster port is enough to completely sway me from saying this game is still worth playing, even with the remake coming in the near future. 

The tl;dr is that while Dead Space isn't the scariest game ever, it's very competently made as an action horror game in the same vein as RE4. I've been replaying a lot of older games and I just had to replay this one.. I am surprised that I haven't reviewed it so here it goes: You play a character named Isaac, who is not equipped with weapons (at first) but is a space engineer. Assigned to a space ship/station whose distress beacon was heard by your company, you arrive to a nightmare situation. Where did the crew go? What happened? These are some of the questions that will be answered as hell unfolds before your (helmet) eyes. The graphics, even since 2007, are still remarkably well done and suit the ambient atmosphere of the game perfectly - I have no complaints. The audio is scary, brooding, and ready to pounce upon your nerves at any moment. Music is largely non-existent but that is a resounding good decision by the developers. What music that is heard is barely distinguishable from the background ambience. This is one of those games that has to be experienced, rather than played. Highly recommended, and certainly worth a replay if it's been a while.

I played Dead Space on release, and for many years I've considered it the greatest sci-fi horror game out there. So for its tenth anniversary I thought it was time for a replay. I can happily report that Dead Space remains a masterpiece of tension, fear and - at times - sheer terror. It holds up on account of its level design, atmosphere, unique enemies and remarkable sound design.

It's worth noting, however, that there are some bugs in this PC port that were never fixed. They're easy to resolve with some minor tweaking, but it's annoying. First off, the in-game vsync creates a nasty lag on the mouse which makes it difficult to aim. Disable it in-game, and enable it using your GPU control panel - it then plays beautifully with a mouse and keyboard (and far more precise than using the controller). Secondly, if you play on fullscreen (which is the default setting) then the in-game brightness becomes way too high. Turn it down to minimum in the in-game settings, and the game looks as dark and moody as intended.

Ok, so that took 5 minutes to resolve. Back to the game. Dead Space takes place almost entirely on the Ishimura, a gothic mining vessel that's a logically-designed place full of interconnections that's almost reminiscent of Dark Souls had Dead Space not come first. Chapter level loads slightly impair this feeling of the Ishimura being a single, cohesive design, but it works in terms of having discretely functional areas. There's a real sense of claustrophobia not only in the place, but in your control of Isaac, a largely silent (he grunts and screams, but never talks) engineer wearing a protective and bulky rig. The feeling that you're alone is overwhelming for much of the time. Isaac's rig is an iconic piece of kit, almost as unwieldy as a mech as you clump around, smashing things underfoot with a visceral (pun intended) crunch and grunt. It feels a little restrictive, but then it's meant to be. Dead Space 2 improved mobility and control which worked better as an action game, but as a horror game the control system here is more effective.

The enemies are straight out of John Carpenter sci-fi horror, human flesh splitting and sprouting a mixture of crab-like appendages, teeth and tentacles. These body horror monstrosities are accompanied by some extremely effective sound design, and their ability to rip you apart in short order makes them genuinely scary. In fact, sound design overall is exceptional. The entire ship feels alive with menace, positional audio making you constantly on edge. Several times I found I had to dial down the tension by turning the volume down, that's how effective it is. If you want the full experience, Dead Space is not a game to play while watching TV or listening to a podcast. Equally effective is the pacing, with scattered "havens" giving you a brief sense of relief before  you have to open a door and head into another area full of horrors. The designers do a smart job of slowly ramping up the stakes, keeping each new encounter interesting, and throwing in regular set-pieces and the occasional environmental puzzle.

Even if you didn't find the atmosphere particularly frightening (in which case my hat is off to your strong constitution), the gameplay stands on its own. Combat is impactful, slicing off limbs to visibly alter the appearance and behaviour of enemies, controlling where the threat is coming from (particularly later in the game) using your abilities and different weapons. Each unique enemy type has its own personality and approach to dealing with it, and later encounters really try to put you into challenging situations trying to deal with them all. Even though the game is set in a space ship, the designers do a good job trying to make each area feel unique and functional. There are places you visit that you'll never want to see again... until you realise that you have to. Admittedly the chase from one task to another, where each problem solved immediately leads to another, can wear a little thin (even the in-game dialogue alludes to this!) but I never felt a sense of fatigue for its entire duration.

RPG elements come into play through the use of power nodes, which can be spent upgrading a variety of weapons and abilities. Power nodes are of course in limited supply and you can't level up everything in a single playthrough, so there are choices to be made. This time I challenged myself to beat the game using only the plasma cutter, the starting weapon. Levelled up this thing is lethal and satisfying, but sadly you don't get an achievement for it in the Steam version.
 
There's no doubt my love for this kind of sci-fi horror strongly influences my feelings towards this game, but there's little doubt this is a classic. The sequel definitely made a lot of improvements to the formula, and many prefer it, but for me the original Dead Space is still the best.

Fucking up has consequences in a game with limited resources. And that tension just makes the game great for me.

Detailed Review:
Dead Space is a 3rd person over the shoulder horror game set in futuristic space. It's garnered a cult following due to it's great use of antagonist. It truly has set the standard for modern horror games.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Everything about Dead Space is in part like homage to old horror games of old. It was the first game to honestly scare me since Silent Hill 2 back in 2001. You play in 3rd person over the shoulder. As it's set in the 26th century, you can expect futuristic tools to compliment your arsenal. Most importantly you have a rail gun, a unique engineering tool that works as your primary weapon. The main antagonists are scarily hard to put down at first which makes the game scary until you learn to adapt towards your foe, which makes the game feel like you're progressing not only through the game towards the plot at the finale, but as a player. The game has a lot of little niches that make you pleasantly surprised for a 2008 game.
[list]
    [*] 3rd Person over the shoulder style gameplay
    [*] Has a lot of unique little perks that keep you pleasantly surprised
    [*] Atmosphere is very movie-esque
    [*] Genuinely scary
    [*] Smooth pacing
    [*] No HUD, helps immerse you into the game where you're not blocked in the screen by menus and boxes
[/list]

[h1]Sound[/h1]
First off, the music creeps me out. It deepens the ambiance to the point where you forget all together that it's a jump-scare tactic. Often the game will play that, much to your dismay, to your disadvantage. In some instances, the music will build up like something will jump out from around the corner to ultimately lead to nothing happening. It kept me on my toes for the majority of my gameplay.
[list]
    [*] Amazing music
[/list]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Takes a great blend of the sci-fi genre with horror atmosphere. Most of the game is set in the dark but it works well and still holds up well to date.

    [*] Creepy environment, things of very movie-esque scene you'd find in the like of Alien+The Thing+Dawn of the Dead
    [*] Creepy enemy design

You should do these two things before playing the game on PC with mouse and keyboard:
1) Don't use the game's vsync feature and use vsync via your graphics driver. The game's own vsync caps the fps to 30 and makes it very unpleasant.
2) Download the Dead Space mouse fix fan patch. The mouse aiming is normally dreadfully bad and this patch makes it perfect.

Those two easily fixable issues aside, this game is so fantastic. I'm not all that familiar with horror games, and I don't think this game is scary in the slightest, but every other aspect of it is top notch.

First, the gameplay. It's absolutely perfect. You have to shoot the Necromorphs' limbs to kill them, then stomp on them to make sure they are dead. The shooting is impactful, satisfying, requires precision and the gore is really good too. There's a lot of weapons that can be bought from the store, though I only used the Plasma Cutter and the Pulse Rifle, both of which were enough.

You have some tools like Stasis and Kinesis, though they are used more often for puzzles than combat. Stasis is used to slow down fast object/enemies, and Kinesis allows you to move objects and throw smaller ones at enemies. These tools make the puzzle sections fun, and though I didn't use them much in combat they were useful in that regard too.

There's a lot of Necromorph types with distinct behaviors. Slashers are the most common ones and are easy to kill, Swarmers constantly leap at you and can be annoying to deal with, Pregnants spawn more enemies if you shoot their belly, and the Exploders might be my favourite type of Necromorph. You can shoot down the explosive they carry to kill them and other enemies around them, and the explosion is glorious. Every now and then there's also the Brute, a miniboss that is very dangerous and makes you want to use Stasis on it to make it more easily manageable.

The presentation of the game is really good too. The graphics on a basic standpoint look good, and the ship has a lot of dark areas and areas filled with fleshy walls that are kinda gross. The most interesting part of the game is the HUD. Instead of it being a typical HUD, it's very different. The player's health and stasis are shown on the back of the suit, video screens are shown in front of Isaac and move with him as he moves etc. It's very innovative.

There's the Zero-Gravity areas which are creative, with you being able to jump from one distant location to another, and enemies like Leapers attack from every direction in those areas. I find them to be some of the most fun parts of the game.

Levels also have parts where you are outside the ship and need oxygen to survive, which gives a sense of tension. Enemies often appear and you want to kill them quickly so you can leave the areas before your oxygen becomes dangerously low. Isaac's exhausted breathing and a lot of things being quiet makes it quite tense.

Enemies and ammo crates give you resources you need, like ammo and weapons, and you can also buy said resources from the shop. There's items that have the sole purpose of giving you more money when you sell them, making you want to look for them. The most important things to buy in the shop are suit upgrades and power nodes. Suit upgrades allow you to carry much more resources, and you can use power nodes for things like increasing your health, making weapons deal more damage and take less time to reload etc. Power nodes also appear in many locations, so it's good to look for them.

The story is... alright. Isaac tries to find his girlfriend over the course of the game, and the other few survivors like Hammond help him. I didn't find any of the characters all that interesting, and Isaac has Gordon Freeman personality. The twist at the end of the game was cool though, and the ending... had something sudden happen out of nowhere.

Boss fights are fun, but they are on the easier side. All of the bosses require you to shoot at yellow parts of their bodies to kill dismember them, and they all can be killed without much trouble. I'd say the hardest boss was the Slug, and that was mainly due to the bad turret controls.

As I said, I find the game to be very lacking in the horror department. It's atmospheric, but not really scary. The game sometimes uses jumpscares that aren't even shocking, and I also didn't find the violent death scenes to be that disturbing.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
Dead Space 1 might be one of the best games I have played in a long time. Lackluster horror and kinda bad story aside, the game is amazing in every aspect. Combat is great, graphics are great and level design is great. The game is outright a masterpiece in my eyes and I recommend it.

After not having played the game for around 10 years I finally replayed Dead Space with one of my friends as a Halloween special this year. This game is an absolute masterpiece from start to finish. What's incredibly funny to me is that the gameplay is based on Resident Evil 4 for the most part (When I first played Dead Space back in the day I hadn't tried RE4) but Dead Space absolutely destroys RE4 in every single way possible with its insane improvements IN MY OPINION. The story and narrative throughout the game is simple yet interesting, as it unravels you'll get a better understanding of what exactly it is you're fighting and why it's so important to the Dead Space universe. Gameplay wise it's amazing, it's intense when it wants to be, has great boss fights, fun mechanics and puzzles to play around with, enough enemy variants to always keep you from getting bored and an upgrade system that allows YOU to pick what you'd like to specialize in. One of the coolest things about Dead Space is by far the atmosphere. You might think for a game that on average lasts about 10-14 hours that the enviorment would get boring but think again! This might be an odd comparison to draw but Dead Space's chapter system kinda reminds me of the level structure in Luigi's Mansion 3 where each floor has its own theme. You see in Dead Space there's a total of 12 chapters each exploring their own section of the Ishimura flagship you find yourself trapped on. Believe it or not but none of these chapters really feel the same, their locations feel unique. One very important thing about this game! DO NOT PLAY IT ON EASY OR NORMAL MODE! Your first playthrough should be on Hard. You might say "That's for me to decide, thank you very much!" Yes of course it is, but Dead Space didn't do a very good job balancing easy and normal mode. On every difficulty below Hard the enemies doesn't feel intimidating, you get way too much ammo, and each fight section just feels like a minor bump on the road. While on hard you'll actually fear for your life when encountering certain types of Necromorphs! ALSO Hard isn't actually that difficult at all. You see Hard mode in Dead Space starts out pretty challenging till you get your first couple of upgrades. Yes the game will be a bit harder in first 2 chapters but after that you're gonna thank yourself for not turning all the enemies into the Grunts from Halo.

Nasty and gory-disgusting, they are rapidly rushing with cannibalistic urge. And you are forced to, in fact, just incapacitate them by cutting of the limbs with space-engineering stuff like a precise plasma cutter, more widespread line cutter or, my favorite, a pipeline saw. Meaning that aiming at center mass or a head won’t work, decapitation even aggravates them more, although you can do that just for the sake of the stopping power effect. Whilst you are about to be crumped by necrophilies you also switching vertical-horizontal aiming modes on the almighty cutter tool - [u]handle with care[/u]. 
In the heat of the moment Isaac's tanky, but not sluggish movement makes outmaneuvering them a class act. However, you can stomp the car wreck victims like a savage with your military grade boots or just hit them with an arm's swipe - obviously risky, but seeing procedural dismemberment makes your inner censor happy. 
To diversify maim-mutilation process the devs can introduce other not necessarily engineer-related stuff like a pulse rifle, flamethrower or a laser-beam gun. I salute this arsenal for not supplying you with a know-how solution. Each weapon comes with an alternative fire, but also with both purpose and shortcomings. You'd think that a pipeline saw capable of temporarily keeping the blades at a distance is OP, but it can make you vulnerable if you are not preserving the needed range. RIfle's 360° fire mode is useful for crowd control, but depletes ammo in seconds.
[quote]Besides the "pew-pew" you can temporarily freeze smth with a [b]stasis[/b] module or grab an object on a certain distance with [b]kinesis[/b]. Overall DS is an easygoing - nervously tangling fun where improvisation can be your lifeblood. It's necro ecosystem makes sure if you utilize all the tools to a great success. The bosses rather bark than bite, but each encounter is a spectacle to behold in vein of God of war's gigantism. 

But the [b]石村[/b] won't fix itself, so cowboy up before the next repair objective revolving around puzzles. The game will push you through mesmerizingly handcrafted decks where everything is thought-out. From med labs with artificially grown babies and nature-sounding orangeries to stark industrial environments where asteroids are decomposed within the power fields. From time to time the level-design opens up to screen saving panoramas in outer space presenting you highly atmospheric zero gravity action with bits of debris floating around. You can even play multistaged space basketball or practice on targets in the security barracks.

For a game using the Godfather engine Dead Space looks impressive, dare i say, timeless if you won't look at the textures under a microscope. It's stellar art direction exemplifies that graphics is nothing by itself, because the design leaves an indelible imprint on it. The enormous technocracy of dieselpunk setting. The all-industrial practically of Issac's suits. Rotted versions of necromorphs with glowing eyes and dark rancid flesh covered in cysts. Not only does Dead Space cleverly uses the interplay between lighting and fog, but refuses to leave you confounded with it's diegetic HUD. The dynamic waypoint trail saves yourself a headache, especially when all falls apart. Dead Head Fred game was the first to put on a back a life indicator, but DS has improved it with various states of health.

Given that this was originally intended to be a System Shock 2's sequel, the horror is not so subtle. You walk through foreboding hallways where everything is orchestered within the game's linear structure. It's cool that necromorphs can hoap out of vents, but i expected it to be random with such amount of spawn points. Some are posing as corpses punishing you for unattentivness. But the game can do better. There are unexpected jumpscares in previously safe areas. Every train ride is a paranoic nightmare due to smoke hiding the enemies. As you uncover the story closer you will usher into horors of your own imagination. [b]The thing[/b] has tampered with the crew's minds so badly that you can stumble upon cryptic messages showcasing unique language, which looks like a mix between ancient greek and hebrew - you can decipher it.
 
The neatest part about DS horror is it's skin-deep sound design, which gels well with everything in the game. With my [b]Beyerdynamic DT 770 PRO[/b] plugged into DAC this was an aural bliss. When the game is not trying to scare your eyes it can do it with noise. Almost everywhere smth around you is happening on the background making prediction of forthcoming events a wild guess. Secluded rooms tells your tales of despair with whispers in your ears, making you reach out for schizo pills. Jason Graves has composed pretty traditional score, but the one which yanks you out of the comfort. Eerie-grimmy cosmic ambient is f@ckn glorious.

Dead Space is a public service announcement warning you to not be one of the first generation explorers and engineers to colonize space. It's one of my favorite horror games and a series I love, a classic that holds up today. Let's take a look at why it works and what separates it from your average "guy shoots aliens" game.

In Space Is Scary you play as An Average Engineer, a man who immediately regrets agreeing to come into work on his day off. You and your crew of exposition dispensers board the USG Ishimura and everything starts breaking. In a cute spin on the usual narrative framing device of early 2000s gaming you actually fix everything to advance through the ship and thus the plot. You are an actual Space Engineer and you have a variety of tools to assist in doing not-at-all mundane tasks that make up the level design and exploration. It may not sound like it makes any difference but I found it subtly charming to have a real reason to be doing crazy dangerous video game action things to get through stages. I was actually restoring power, fixing the flux capacitors and feeling justified in going through these OSHA nightmares. It can be difficult to identify genuine charm but Dead Space has it. It feels right in a delightful way that almost all of your guns are repurposed mining tools and although not perfect the Ishimura feels like a place where people actually lived, making surveying the aftermath of the end all the better.

The stars of the show are the necromorphs, our alien antagonists. These guys are a treat. You know these boys are well designed when they're able to go against one of horrors most common rules: don't show the monster too early/often, if at all. The necromorphs show up frequently yet are always intimidating, always threatening, always meaningful. Even as you advance into late game stages you will find some new threat that makes you flinch, whether it is bodies repurposed to spread airborne particles that moan awfully as they do it, the creepy crawling head guys and infectors that are actually easier to fight but nastier to witness or the unerring Hunter, reigning king of unsettling. Dead Space uses powerful sound design and potent art design to pitch a foe that is unnerving even with dated graphics. Smart map design lets the necromorphs flank or swarm you and turn wide open spaces into claustrophobic invitations to match any corner or tunnel, for hearing but not seeing enemies is a terrible prospect. They come in a wide variety, they can come out of the vents and in the series trademark twist they are not playing by zombie rules, each type having different sweet spots that incentivize dismemberment, lending Dead Space a good gameplay motivation of seeking weak spots that syncs up with in-universe rules. Like the Space Engineer level design this smoothly improves player immersion.

Throughout each Dead Space game I find myself wonderfully immersed. I am scared and on edge yet not psychologically rattled. Dead Space is heavier on the action side of things and by game's end you will be filled with a bit more courage than not. But each time I entered the armor shop tube and came out in my new armor, each time I confronted a build up to a new danger spot or big boss fight and underwent the ritual of checking and reloading each of my guns, each time I thought I was advancing down a hallway and something terrible and in-universe happened and I had to react... I realized Dead Space had drawn me in perfectly. The soft terror of the setting and the budding madness of man and marker is a mirror to the moment to moment action of fighting the necromorphs, a textbook execution of highs and lows that enhance one another. Dead Space is great design for a great game and I strongly recommend it.

[i]I take a deep breath. Come on, I tell myself, it's just another corner. You can't just stay here, wherever "here" is on this endlessly large and chaotic ship. And anyway, they'll come for you, sooner or later, here or there, so you might as well just go. Still, it takes all my resolve to move on, carefully aiming the welder straight ahead, expecting to be jumped at any moment now.[/i]

Dead Space is the single most horrifying game I've ever played. It uses all the familiar horror tropes - isolation, darkness, the unknown, delusion, overwhelming odds, mistrust - and manages to not only make them believable in a sci-fi setting, but so visceral that they'll grip the player from the moment they set foot on the Ishimura. 

[i]Nothing. Long corridors of nothing. Nothing but the noises, the creaks, the constant tension, the flickering lights, the many, many wall panels, each and every one fit to hide one of the horrors that crawl through the intestines of this ship, that have infected it to the core. And when they finally catch up with me, as they inevitably will, it still, STILL comes as a surprise, sending me frantically pacing backwards every time, aiming for... anything. Heads, limbs, whatever it is that keeps these monsters alive.[/i]

Between all the scares and darkness, Dead Space also manages to be beautiful, almost transcendent at times. The quiet, damaged, empty bridge of the Ishimura, with its high glass panes, looking out into infinite space, for example, allowing you a moment of peace after encountering something that almost would've been the end of your journey. 

[i]Space is peaceful, quiet, soothing, but it's a deceptive peace, trying to lower my defenses, distract me from the dangers that lurk all around me, just waiting or a chance to get to me. But... it's so beautiful. So calm. Can't I, just for a moment, rest among the stars, forget about the nightmare I'm in? Just for a moment...[/i]

Even after all this time that I've played this game, I feel myself on occasion thinking back on it, remembering pieces, scenes, locations, sometimes dreaming about it. It's not often that anything gets under my skin like that, but Dead Space certainly did.

[h1] Retro Review[/h1] 
Dead space was in a time where I was still a kid and actually feared horror games. I played this sometimes on my brothers pc, and barely remember finishing it, mostly because it was still horrifying to me to play games like this. This changed now, although I still get jumpscared at times, but the constant dreadful atmosphere doesn’t catch me in the same way any more. I love horror games mostly only if combat is involved, rather than being a walking simulator. And unlike the static resident evil esque isometric games where combat is rather serviceable and only there to add the dread of item scarcity here the combat is actually a proper main and good part of the game.

[u] Gameplay[/u] 
As a third person shooter your character moves relatively slow and has a certain weight behind him, aiming is still very responsive and snappy. You have your main weapon, a sort of electric cutter that sends a beam out that cuts anything in its path. Which is the starting weapon and strangely I found the best one in the entire game. There are other weapons and ammo types, but most weapons I found are either just fun to use or very niche, like the flamethrower being very neat for small hard to hit enemies but useless for the rest. 

Since the main feature of the game is that cutting off limbs damages them the most those weapons who feature cutting are actually the best in the game, aside those enemies that have clear glowing weakpoints and can be easily attacked with others. I think this balancing of the game is really great. Additionally to counter the lack of movement of the main character you can throw items or slow enemies or things down via a stasis module. This also works together and makes most of the puzzles. The puzzles arent hard, sometimes a bit creative but really nice to change the pace in this game.

The puzzles and anything else on the ship is dangerous and wants you dead, this concludes in very neat death animation and action sequences. Its mainly a horror game but also feels closely to an action roller coaster. For me it was the best combination between both. There are also some space or zero gravity sequences, which were okay, but nothing impressive.

Traversing the map is really great due to the great map and waypoint system the game has included. You can find anything you want easily even though the map is rather full of corridors and such. This makes the map not as recognizable as it could be, but definitely fits the setting and makes the more unique map pieces more memorable. 

Also neat is the upgrading system where you slowly upgrade your suit or weapon by finding various resources in boxes that you can stomp open with the best stomping animation ive seen so far. Although I personally found the game even on very hard quite easy on the resources at times.

The major issue of this game is the performance, as you need to do a variety of fixes and its not just as easy as downloading a simple patch like with some other older games. This can also create some new or show old bugs. Meh.

[u]Story [/u] 
The main character is an engineer and follows a check-up on some ship that stopped responding, where apparently the whole crew is missing and monsters appear around every corner. The protagonist also has personal stakes as his girlfriend is somewhere on this ship. You don’t really feel that much connection between those two as you only start with a video clip of her, but the main part of the story is rather living through this and discovering why exactly the passengers turned into monsters, additionally exploring and discovering about this sci-fi universe as you luckily wont get bombarded with exposition dumps.

[u]Aesthetics [/u] 
Despite its age the game looks really fantastic, mostly due to its really good lighting, that if the lighting does suck at times it reveals its age and low textures. Most known and impressive is this game for its hud and information the game shows the player quite naturally via pop ups and holograms on the characters suit or menus he opens.

Although the OST wasnt really memorable to me, it did its job really well, giving you a cascade of sounds that increase the distress during action moments. Mostly the gun effects and sound effects of enemies have been engraved into my ears. Especially the environmental stuff sounds good and I prefer this definitely more than having a banger soundtrack in such a game.

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR [/u] 
Definitely worth to check out and the cheaper alternative towards the remake to play a neat action/horror survival hybrid that doesn’t ever go over the top with its action parts. The universe they created is quite credible and the story intriguing. The combat is fun and it offers a good mix between this and the puzzle parts to change up the pace. There isn't much I can complain aside the abundance of resources and the various fixes you have to do in order to get it to run properly on windows 10.#

Fantastic survival horror game

Dead Space 1 is still a classic game that'll have you on the edge of your seat all the way through. [spoiler]Even when you become a necromorph killing machine by the end of the game[/spoiler], you'll still feel unnerved just by walking around on the Ishimura. The game is a real gem of survival horror game design.

I played Dead Space 1 after only playing Dead Space 3 on the Xbox 360 a few years back, so I was interested to see how much changed between the games. Dead Space 1 is a much tighter experience than Dead Space 3. The levels, while linear, don't feel that way with plenty enough to explore and look at. The environmental story telling is on another level with this game too. Piecing the story of the Ishimura through audio logs and context clues is a real treat. Each section of the ship filled me with dread as I trudged down them corridors. The game still holds up graphically and auditorily thanks to its striking aesthetics and foreboding sound design. Even by the end of the game when I had thought I'd seen all the games tricks I still felt intimidated walking around by my lonesome.

The gameplay, while a tad bit dated (make sure to install the mouse fix mod) still holds up well. The game has a solid gameplay loop of fighting, exploring, and scavenging with some light puzzle solving to break up the pace. The difficulty of the game on normal - while a bit on the easy side - definitely is still challenging enough to provide a good bit of fun. Each enemy requires a different way of handling them, even if you're only using the plasma cutter. Every enemy I fought had me thinking "How do I most efficiently take this monster apart?" Some enemies even change how you explore around because of what they do. The stomp is also one of the best things ever put into a video game.

[h1] Sweat Face [/h1]

Man... first of all... I had a lot of fun playing this game.

Dead Space is such a refreshing experience to beheld, especially as the majority of horror games I've played recently have been nothing but downright disappointing & felt unfocused.
Luckily however, you can never go wrong with a classic.



[h1] Headstomp [/h1]

The game-play of Dead Space is really, really good! Not perfect -- but reaching 'fantastic'!
I f#cking adored cutting limbs off for a continuous entire campaign, it never got old. It was just super thrilling. But when it reached the point where the mechanic begun to feel a tad stale... the game ended. The game does not feel so short that you ultimately didn't get to master the mechanics, nor did it feel so long that it eventually became monotonous to play. The game knows its own limits, it knows that it isn't something that should go on, and on, and on, and on, and on... not for the sake of your attention... nor for your heart...

I really enjoyed the level-design in this game. Sure, there are a few occasional of "meh" rooms. But they're gone in less than 5 minutes anyways.
I loved how the first-half of the game starts off really cramped & claustrophobic; making you feel truly uncomfortable. But that alone isn't enough to evoke the spine-chilling in fear in gamers, no. The fear of the cramped hallways & tightly-constructed open areas are horrifying due to the enemies.
The monsters in this game are horrifying. They're crazy... f#cking fast !! If they run at you, you have to react fast! They'll catch up to you in no time, and they'll tear you apart limb by limb if these beautifully satisfying grotesque death-animations if they ever get their claws unto you. The monsters are mean, and not afraid to f#ck you up. Their AI feels almost truly otherworldly. They run at you like no other predator would. They only have one instruction, and that is to [b] KILL [/b] you! They can't think of anything else, they don't care about anything else. It's just "I am coming right at you, I am killing you. I will kill you." It's super scary! It's super cool! 
But as your arsenal grows, your stats raise, your skills better; the game's areas begin to open up to true arenas. They feel a lot more open -- and while that would seem like a negative to some, it's to really test your skills by cramping you not with tightly cramped hallways... no. It's to cramp you with tightly cramped bundles of enemies at once. You'll end up having to run around & shift attention from one enemy to the other swiftly, as your positions in combat change, not just by you, but from the enemies as well. Especially as the monsters will literally hop out of vents behind you to surprise attack you meanwhile as you're dead-set focused on another enemy.

Your slow camera prevents you from playing the game like you're the DoomGuy. If there's an enemy behind you, you don't just turn around & shoot it. You run. It's all about getting out of their attack-distance! You don't have time to turn around, unless you want to be turned into a lump of dead meat.

I adore trying to shakily shoot the limbs off of the monsters as they run at me full-speed!
As enemies have thin & often quick-moving limbs it can make aiming at them super difficult, especially when they're either running at you or is in your face clawing your chest wide open!
You will constantly feel like you don't have enough ammo & resources to deal with enemies, but you always will, because the game will make sure of it. You're always treading on the fine-line in-between "ammo" & "no ammo". You'll run around a lot -- especially late-game on 'hard' difficulty -- carefully switching between weapons in a hurry as to optimize your resources, because you need to, because if you don't you will not have ammo for the guns you might need soon after; and therefore can lead to your death.

I too adore how the """weapons""" you find during this game are so clearly supposed to resemble as if they were actually just ordinary construction tools made for working purposes, reused as a defensive method. Super cool!
this reflects upon your abilities too!
It's really immersive, and reminds you that Isaac is no more than a mere engineer using whatever he can mange to scavenge to survive. This is further reflected in this punch & stomp animations. He's an incapable man. He doesn't know how to punch like a action-movie hero. He's just some guy.
When he punches it's clear he's just giving it his all to survive. He's just punching as hard as he can to hopefully survive, meanwhile stuck in a suit that probably weighs a truckload to walk around in... and the exact same with the stomp animation.
I am frothing in my mouth over this, this is amazing!



[h1] Horror [/h1]

Grass grows, birds fly, sun shines, and brother?... Dead Space is a scary game.
[b] duh [/b]

I adore how this game uses horror. it doesn't always stick with the principles of it, it doesn't rely on formulaic ideas. It does some wild sh!t & hopes the player gets scared. And that's what makes it scary, as we can never really expect as to what's next.
And while there are a handful of common tropes used, no doubt. They're welcome, as when clustered alongside uncommon tropes they themselves become uncommon with the commons. It earns it, it deserves it.
This is further pushed by the fact that when you die, it's not just some screamer [b] IN YOUR FACE [/b] type of deal. No it just smoothly takes away your control to watch Isaac die horrifically. The fact that you've died -- likely to an enemy that surprised you -- is already a scare enough.
And the smart use of lighting is just downright beautiful too. Not only am I a sucker for good sound-design in games, but I am a sucker for old video-game lighting.
And the atmosphere & mood is just as creepy & f#cked up now, as it were upon release. The graphics still looks great, and the environments look gorgeously grotesque <3

Great game, held back by being a poor port.
It's clear EA doesn't care about [b] THIS [/b] Dead Space anymore. It is only pushed unto PC for some easy extra bucks. Whatever.
But man whoever did the port should feel ashamed.
It's playable, sure. Yeah. Totally. But it is embarrassing at least. It's nowhere near 'Gun' or 'Prince of Persia' bad PC port -- dog bless. At least I can [b] PLAY [/b] this game.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Dead Space is a 'must-play' type of game, and I heftily would recommend playing it. Although if you have to option to rather play it on Xbox 360/Playstation 3; then I would advise for that.

Dead Space is a survival horror game. You are slow moving with jump out and scare you moments. The character Issac controls slow and clunky. Plus your character Issac Clark takes up a lot of the screen, which I guess happens in a lot of over the shoulder shooters. You want to see what's behind you. Since this is an over the shoulder shooter, things can easily sneak up on your left side, even more so than behind you.

The game drips with atmosphere, horror and gore, but it doesn't feel scary. Maybe I'm just used to horror games, or maybe its the fact when you run through a dead enemy, you kick it like a soccer ball and it flops like a rag doll fish. That's probably why Doom 3 had its dead enemies burn into nothing. With Dead Space, the idea is that enemies can still be alive... when they look dead. The game looks awesome and makes great use of lighting and shadow. You won't be in dark areas so much as dim areas with lights shining through vents. It has a great look to it.

Dead Space boasts strategic dismemberment, such as first cutting off a leg of an enemy, before you cut off its head. If you cut off its head, it will blindly swing at you. If you cut off its leg, it will crawl and lunge at you. Most enemies are like this. Other enemies might explode with smaller, more annoying enemies if you're inaccurate. There are also reanimating enemies that take priority, because they'll monsterfy every dead body in the room. So if you're the type of gamer that likes aim over put more bullets into it, this game is for you! The enemies will even work their way through vents if you've gone to another room and they'll pop out. The vents are pretty easy to spot, but a lot of vents are on the ceiling. 

There are four major weapons in the game, the line cutter, flame thrower, plasma rifle and some sort of saw gun. It is unfortunate that you'll end up primarily using the weapon you start with for the entire game. That feels like a wasted opportunity. The flame thrower feels extremely weak if not completely useless.

You're able to collect items, like health, ammo, air canisters for when you're walking in space and its all contained in your limited inventory. When you upgrade your 'rig' (suit), you can carry more stuff, but for the most part, since everything is sellable, you'll rarely run out of room. As the game starts, there is plenty of ammo, but at around six hours in, ammo gets scarce, but you can still buy more. Lack of ammo comes from missing vulnerable points of enemies and having them explode into smaller points.

You'll also pick up node modules to upgrade things and if you start upgrading your line cutter, then why would you ever switch to a different weapon? Plus, any ammo that you get for other weapons, you can just sell at one of the game's stores for credits that you can use to buy more line cutter ammo. There are locked rooms that you can use a node to get into, but since nodes are one of the most valuable and costly items in the game, it might not be worth the risk to see what's in the mystery room. You'll also be able to explore and find items in cabinets, lockers and smashable boxes, but you really can't wander too far off the beaten path.

Traversing the USG Ishimura feels like there is plenty of back tracking, with some getting lost. Luckily there is a 3D slightly difficult to use map. For the most part, each level is contained into branching segments, you'll start at the root of the map tree, clear out one branch and all of its limbs, end up at the root / hub of the level, then go for the next branch area. Sadly some of the 'chapters' reuse levels. The USS Ishimura is a big space ship, and I would call it similar to Metroid-Vania-ish since you'll revisit areas of a ship, but its all broken into 'chapters' that you can't return to unless its in the storyline to return to that section.

There are some puzzles, but nothing major. You'll get powers like telekinesis to move objects and a slow down stasis to solve puzzles and get through areas. Without the puzzles, the game seems easy even on normal difficulty.

The game has a very painful key binding system, especially for lefties. While you can rebind keys, you can't rebind all keys, so I recommend just using a controller. The controller works great and has simple controls for a complex system. You've got buttons for run, inventory, aim, stomp (to downed enemies and boxes), melee attack (which seems useless), use button and the D-pad will call your 4 weapons to switch. When you're aimed at something, you can reload, fire your weapon. alt-fire, use telekinesis or stasis to slow anything down.

Thankfully save points and checkpoints are everywhere. It keeps the game progressing, but another negative of the game is when you run out of ammo or health and just can't pass a section, you're locked into that section. When you're stuck, you've got two choices, run all the way back to a store at the start of a level, or sometimes you might just have to restart from a save point. This is why I can understand EA's desire to throw micro transactions into the game. If you get stuck with no ammo, no credits and only have 1 save file, you might literally have to restart the game. When you get 10+ hours in, that will kill your desire to play.

In all, the game feels good to play, despite how slow it is. If you enjoy typical space horror with the plot of Aliens, this game is for you! The game has been $5 on Steam and free on Origin. Chances are if you wait, there will be a sale, a bundle or a free download.

Dead Space has some issues on modern hardware, especially with mouse sensitivity and frame rate. Here’s how to fix it and also have better visuals:

Guide to fixing mouse sensitivity problems:

NVIDIA Control Panel:
• Go to Manage 3D Settings, then Program Settings, and select Dead Space.
• Set Max Frame Rate to 60 FPS.
• Turn Vertical Sync on.
• Set Power Management Mode to Prefer maximum performance.
• Turn Low Latency Mode on.

In-game settings:
• Launch the game and go to the video settings.
• Turn V-Sync off (even though it’s on in the Control Panel; this fixes mouse issues).
• Choose a resolution that runs at 60 Hz. The game shows the refresh rate next to each option.

Guide for better visuals (recommended for mid or high-end PCs):

NVIDIA Control Panel:
• Set Antialiasing Mode to Enhance the application setting.
• Set Antialiasing Setting to 2x.
• Set Transparency to 4x.
• Turn on Antialiasing Gamma Correction.
• Turn on FXAA.
• In Global Settings, enable DSR at 2.25x DL. This gives you higher resolution options with better image quality and no performance loss. 

Additional tips: If you have a high-end PC, you could increase both Antialiasing Setting and Transparency to 8x as well as set Negative LOD Bias to "Clamp". These are all in the Program Settings. Texture Filtering - Quality: High Quality and maximum performance for Power Management Mode in Global Settings could also be great. These settings weren't tested in my playthrough but should yield good results.

One more small tip: change the in-game sound mode to 5.1 surround for better audio quality.

That's about it for notes.

Dead Space is a third-person sci-fi horror game where you play as Isaac Clarke, an engineer who is part of a team sent to help repair a mining vessel called the USG Ishimura. Things seem fairly normal at first, but it soon becomes apparent that far more has gone wrong on the Ishimura than mere technical difficulties. The team gets ambushed by horrifying mutated monsters called Necromorphs, created from human corpses. Isaac, wearing an engineer’s outfit and armed with a plasma cutter mining tool, must fight these horrid creatures as he navigates his way through the ship, trying to find a way off of it and also getting to the bottom of the nightmare that it’s become. 

The first thing this game deserves huge praise for is the UI. It’s perfect, literally perfect, the best in any game I’ve ever played, fully integrated into the game’s world and very clear. Isaac’s health is shown as a glowing spine, a part of his RIG suit, with a Stasis meter next to it. Weapons show ammo via holographic readouts. Inventory, maps, objectives, and logs all appear as holographic screens. There’s even a holographic oxygen meter that appears behind Isaac’s head in areas with no oxygen. Everything here is immersive and free of clutter. I should also mention that there’s a very handy “breadcrumb” system that shows you where you need to go if you get lost, appearing as holographic lines that are projected from Isaac’s suit, which is wonderful. Crates, lockers or doors you can open are shown with either a blue or red light, blue for accessible and red for not. Again, this is wonderful.

Another thing I want to commend Dead Space for is the atmosphere. It’s incredible, the Ishimura is rife with messages scrawled onto the walls by terrified crew members as well as being strewn with bloody corpses (many of them dismembered and/or horribly disfigured), blood stains, flickering lights; some crew members even being fused into the fleshy walls of the monstrosity that has taken over the ship while still alive and in unimaginable agony, etc. Not to mention many gloomy environments and eerie ambience adding to the terrifying atmosphere. This really is a game you should play in the evening, in a quiet room with the lights off, playing with headphones. For a 2008 game, it looks and sounds amazing and has aged very well. Every part of the Ishimura you visit is unique and interesting. For example, there are science labs that include tanks with babies in them, gardens where vegetables and fruits are grown, a mining deck where asteroids are broken down for metal ore, etc. All of these are environments that are memorable and distinct and made me excited to see what the next areas would look like. 

The gameplay is brilliant: scavenging, exploration, and frequent Necromorph encounters make for an enjoyable and thrilling experience. The aim mode intentionally lowers mouse sensitivity to heighten tension. You also have a Stasis ability that slows enemies (at the cost of limited energy) as well as a Kinesis ability that can lift and hurl objects like the Gravity Gun in Half-Life 2. The enemy variety in this game is great and makes the combat dynamic, urging you to employ different tactics. Slashers are basic melee enemies, meanwhile Leapers and Lurkers can crawl on walls and ceilings, Leapers pouncing at you and Lurkers firing barbs at you from a distance. Exploders carry explosive sacs that blow up if shot or in close proximity to Isaac. There are many more, but I suggest you discover them yourself. 

The combat in this game focuses largely on limb dismemberment rather than simple body or head shots like in many other games. Isaac’s weapons, particularly the Plasma Cutter and Line Gun, make this apparent. Each weapon has two firing modes. The Plasma Cutter can be fired horizontally or vertically, adding versatility. The Line Gun fires wide arcs of plasma, and its alt-fire mode shoots energy mines. Not all weapons are for cutting limbs, though. The Flamethrower is a decent crowd-control option, particularly against small enemies like Swarmers. Fireballs are its alt-fire mode, making it usable at longer ranges. The Contact Beam shoots potent long-range energy blasts and has a shockwave as an alt-fire mode, in case foes get too close. There are other weapons as well: the Force gun, Ripper, and Pulse Rifle, but I wasn’t a fan of them and wouldn’t recommend them personally. Isaac does have a couple melee attacks but they’re very basic and should only be used as a last resort when enemies get too close. The stomp is great for opening supply crates, though, so use it often.

The story is very engaging, you encounter many text and audio logs, giving you a better idea of what was happening on the Ishimura before you arrived. There are also twists and turns in the plot that keep things exciting and memorable. The worldbuilding is also really interesting, especially as it delves into a mysterious religion called Unitology. 

As great as this game is, it does have flaws. For instance, the Zero-G movement system is awkward and disorienting quite often and the game doesn’t do a great job explaining it at first. For all other tutorials, the game has a voice over and pop-up message telling you what to do, however, for Zero-G, it’s just a brief pop-up with no voice over, which is strange. Would’ve been better if they just had it be a free-flight mode instead of having to point at something and jump to it using CTRL. I’ve already mentioned that three of the weapons to choose from are unsatisfying to use. These weapons felt poorly designed, not really giving me an incentive to experiment with them in any potential future playthroughs, which I feel is a missed opportunity. The bosses were mostly decent, but one of them is just a turret section, which felt quite underwhelming. There are no hotkeys for using Stasis energy packs or oxygen canisters, which is bizarre considering there’s a hotkey for using health packs. This was apparently done to create “tension”, but it’s just frustrating more than anything. Other than that, I don’t have much else to complain about.

In conclusion, Dead Space is a fantastic game that feels like some of the best elements of Alien and John Carpenter’s The Thing brought together to create a truly unique and unforgettable sci-fi horror experience. 

Final verdict: 8.8/10 “Make us whole again.”

The story behind Dead Space takes place hundreds of years in the future, during a time when mankind has exhausted all of the natural resources on Earth. Fortunately, in this dire time, humanity has mastered space travel, and a process known as planet cracking has been developed to combat this drought. A celestial body is split into pieces, and its minerals are strip-mined and melted, returning the byproducts to Earth for consumption. An entire fleet of ships sails the stars performing these tasks, and the crown jewel of this mining fleet is the USG Ishimura, which has performed more planet cracks that any other vessel. However, on a routine mission, the ship cuts off all communication from galactic command, which is somewhat strange. To discover what's going on, a small maintenance crew is quickly dispatched to the Ishimura from a nearby vessel. 




Players step into the boots of Isaac Clarke, a systems engineer that's part of the dispatched maintenance crew. Outside of fixing the communications issues, Isaac has a number of reasons for arriving on the Ishimura -- he has a number of friends that are stationed on the ship, including someone very special to him that sends an urgent holovid with a few cryptic messages before she disappears. Unfortunately for Isaac and his crew, shortly after they arrive on board the crippled vessel, all hell breaks loose. Their craft is destroyed, leaving them stranded on the Ishimura. The crew is attacked by nightmarish creatures known as Necromorphs, who kill most of Isaac's team and separate him from the surviving members. Even worse, the ship and its systems have started to be corrupted or are failing thanks to the Necromorphic infestation. It's up to Isaac to wander the halls, search for any friends or survivors that are still alive, and fix as many problems as he can until he can find a way to escape the ship, which can take you 12 or more hours to complete. 
Isaac isn't the typical hero that you'd find in most sci-fi games; he doesn't walk into the Ishimura packing a firearm or grenades, nor does he have specialized training. Apart from the first one that Isaac finds on a workbench, all of Isaac's weaponry and items are found via schematics that are scattered across the ship. Only one of them is a true firearm -- the security pulse rifle; the rest of his "guns" are repurposed pieces of mining equipment used for planet cracking. However, Isaac can use his engineering knowledge to make these weapons much more powerful by analyzing their blueprints and rewiring them at workbenches with the use of power nodes. Thanks to these nodes, Isaac can improve their performance in a number of ways, such as carrying more rounds, shortening his reload time, or increasing their damage. This upgrade system even expands to Isaac's space suit, which can be improved to strengthen his suit's armor or his air supply in case he enters a vacuum. He can even use the nodes to augment the stasis or kinesis modules, which can be used to freeze monsters as they charge him or propel items into the creatures, respectively. What's creative about this system is that players won't be able to max out every weapon or every bit of gear that they have in one playthrough; this forces them to choose what they'll specialize in as they go through the ship. 

 
Cleaning house with a little fire.
This is an important decision to make, particularly because some weapons are more effective against the Necromorphs than others, and since you'll need to use strategic dismemberment to weaken and effectively kill them, the right weapon in the right situation can be the fine line between life or death in the game. See, unlike monsters in other games, Necromorphs will shrug off direct attacks to the head or chest and keep coming for more. Blasting their limbs off is the only way to cause enough damage to kill these beasts, and you'll frequently need to focus on aiming accurately and quickly at these weak spots before you're surrounded and dissected yourself. This is particularly true in later stages, when some of the Necromorphs start moving faster than before, and it frequently turns battles into brutal affairs, with severed arms and legs flying everywhere as you attempt to survive the onslaught of creatures. Thanks to the over-the-shoulder, third-person perspective, this can add an extra level of tension to the game while you're fending off swarms of beasts, but be forewarned: there is no quick turnaround command. While some people may consider this to be a problem, this is actually a wise design decision because it makes you feel much more vulnerable and claustrophobic within the confines of the suit, and whether you're moving through a hallway covered in bodies or floating in a zero gravity environment, you always feel as though something could reach out and kill you at any time.

[h1][u]The Short and Sweet[/u][/h1]
Almost everyone that knows horror has heard of Dead Space before. Although it is getting on in years, and its legacy has been tarnished somewhat with the disaster of Dead Space 3, the original game made a large impact for a very good reason.

Dead Space is a third-person shooter horror game, with a large focus on building an oppressive atmosphere without compromising the gunplay and enjoyment of the game in the slightest. Players step into the engineering suit of Isaac Clarke, a member of the emergency response team sent to investigate and repair the USG Ishimura mining vessel. The situation quickly spirals out of control, with the team coming under attack from alien flesh-puppets, the Necromorphs. Isaac, with the help of the surviving members from both the response team and USG Ishimura, must attempt to fix the Ishimura and escape the outbreak without being killed and turned into a Necromorph themselves.

The shooting action is focused around the dismemberment of enemies, as shooting off the limbs of a shambling corpse is more likely to stop it than simply pumping the dead torso full of bullets. This forces the player to stand and aim their weapons, which may be the last thing they want to do when faced with such gruesome and swarming enemies. The game provides a decent number of weapons to assist in this mechanic, with some more competent than others, but players can pick which four they want to bring with them.

 [b][u]Pros[/u][/b]
[list]
[*] The game builds a wonderfully suspenseful atmosphere using a player’s anticipation against themselves, along with fantastic sound design and visual cues. 

[*] The emphasis on dismemberment gives more satisfaction to a player than they would get from simply shooting a faceless grunt in the chest a few times before moving on. 

[*] The story has enjoyable twists, with more being organically revealed to the player as they progress. 
[/list]

[b][u]Cons[/u][/b]
[list]
[*] The blueprints required to add an item to the store can only be found once per game, in specific locations. There is no backtracking to previous levels, meaning that missing a blueprint permanently locks you out of buying that item for the entire game.

[*] There is a beefy list of potential problems a person can experience while trying to run Dead Space. I do not believe these are deal-breakers, but do require some fiddling. See the Technical section below for more details.

 [*] If you are easily disgusted or grossed out by gore or blood, do not play Dead Space. This game contains gratuitous amounts of body horror, disgusting scenery, and blood. Be forewarned before purchasing.
[/list]

[h1]Short Conclusion: An Essential Experience [/h1]

[h1][u]In-Depth Analysis[/u][/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Dead Space, despite being a horror game, provides Isaac with an array of weapons with one unifying factor; all are designed for dismemberment and decapitation. Laser sights on all the weapons show you precisely where they are aiming, and this allows them to more easily target a Necromorph’s appendages, which causes more damage to them than simply peppering them with bullets. 

Ammo is scarce, but just common enough to give you enough rounds to deal with Necromorphs, assuming they don’t waste it. In addition to this, players may only carry four types of weapons at a time, restricting them somewhat. However, players will only find ammunition for weapons they are currently carrying, and not weapons they either don’t own or are in storage. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2136517507

The player’s weapons can be upgraded at specific work tables using power nodes. These upgrades can range from damage and firing speed to capacity and reload speed. Power nodes are found throughout the game, but can also be bought from the store for $10,000 at any time. Money is a critical asset to Isaac, and the difference between a few power nodes or rounds of ammo can be an agonizing choice sometimes.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2136521256

The store requires blueprints found lying around to add new items to the selection, but this has both a positive and a negative. This encourages players to look around for blueprints, ammo, and power nodes, but blueprints are one-time deals. If, for example, you miss the blueprint for Large Health Packs, and then move on to the next level, you will never find that blueprint again and can never buy that item from the store for your entire playthrough. This is a bit too punishing for players, but nearly all blueprints are very easy to find.

 [h1]Story[/h1]
The story is interesting and simple. Isaac finds himself stranded along with his crew inside the USG Ishimura, and must try to find ways to prevent various systems on the ship from failing and killing them all, while simultaneously trying to find a way to escape. As the plot progresses, the story becomes more fanatical, dealing with the cult of Unitology and the source of the grotesque Necromorphs. I will avoid spoilers, even though the game is over a decade old, but I wholly enjoyed the story and character from start to finish.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
Dead Space came out in 2008 and it shows. While the art direction is fantastic and gross, with a nice twist on futuristic machinery and the Necromorphs themselves, the actual graphics are quite dated and rough edges can be seen everywhere. If this does not bother you, you will enjoy what you see.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2136519510

The level design is also designed to cause tension, with many Necromorphs appearing from behind corners or even the player themselves. Any player learns early on that enemies can emerge from ventilation shafts, which causes them to fear vents in the future, but there are innumerable vents throughout the game, which never let you calm down for fear a Necro may suddenly come smashing through one.

[h1]Audio[/h1]
Dead Space uses audio to enhance the suspense tenfold. Scratches inside the vents can indicate an incoming attack, the howl of a Necromorph can cause fear, and the oppressive silence of space walking can allow enemies to sneak up on an unsuspecting player.

The voice acting is very good as well, with some respectable passion behind the roles. The effort the actors put in really help in further immersing a player, the ultimate goal of Dead Space; to immerse, terrify, and excite.

[h1]Technical[/h1]
There are three key potential problems a player can experience in Dead Space:

Mouse acceleration is permanently enabled and has no disable option available. This can make aiming and walking a massive ordeal.

Some players report crazy physics problems if V-Sync is not enabled, but V-Sync itself permanently caps the game at 30fps or lower, which is headache-inducing. I personally didn’t experience any bad problems at 60fps, but some other players report being unable to beat certain physics puzzles.

Hitting “Continue” instead of “Load Game” can knock your difficulty down by one stage (Hard to Normal, Normal to Easy) without indicating it. 

All of these problems have detailed guides on how to fix them and I highly advise you look into it if you want to play the game. I personally only had to fix the mouse acceleration issue, and nothing else. 

 [h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Dead Space is without a doubt one of the best horror games ever made, and a must-play for anyone that enjoys horror and shooting action. The efforts taken to immerse the player are unreal and completely successful, creating an experience like no other that satisfies from every possible perspective. It only suffers slightly from age, and nothing else.
